episode_title: Remembering Paulien Cornelisse, and the border checks end
description: The Netherlands mourns writer and comedian Paulien Cornelisse, who has died at 50 while still on TV every night. The temporary border checks have ended, MPs push back on taxing small savers, mortgage rates hit a high for the year, and prosecutors get tougher on attacks against public workers. Plus a Van Gogh that could break records, a chip shop's queues and house prices, and ideas for the weekend in Amsterdam.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The Netherlands has lost one of its funniest, sharpest voices. Writer and comedian Paulien Cornelisse has died at fifty, while she was still on TV every night.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And in The Hague, MPs are pushing back on a plan that would have hundreds of thousands of small savers paying tax on their savings.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It's Thursday, the first of October. I'm Maya.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And I'm Sam. This is Dutch Daily Briefing.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: We start with Paulien Cornelisse. She died of cancer on Wednesday at the Antoni van Leeuwenhoek, the cancer hospital in Amsterdam. She was fifty, and her loved ones were with her. Sam, for anyone new here, who was she?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: A sort of national language-watcher, with a comedian's timing. Her breakthrough was a 2009 book called Taal is zeg maar echt mijn ding. Roughly, 'Language is, like, totally my thing.' It sold seven hundred thousand copies.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: What was it about?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: How people really talk. Filler words, office jargon, the little things we say without meaning them. She was also a cabaretière, which here means a comedian doing one-person theatre shows. And she wrote absurd books about a confused guinea pig who works in an office.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Last year her essay for the national Book Week sold out on its second day. That had never happened before.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: But most people knew her from TV. Every weeknight she was the one-person jury on De Slimste Mens, 'The Smartest Person', one of the country's most-watched quiz shows.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Those episodes were recorded before the summer. Chemotherapy had made her hair fall out, and she didn't want a wig, so she wore a hat or a cap in every one.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The broadcaster, KRO-NCRV, dropped Wednesday's episode after talking with her family. The rest move back a day. She was also due back on stage at the DeLaMar theatre in Amsterdam in late October. That show's been cancelled, and ticket holders will get refunds.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Prime Minister Rob Jetten called her 'sharp, funny and incredibly kind.' The show's host, Herman van der Zandt, said she was wonderfully energetic, even between treatments.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Her last column in de Volkskrant ran just a week ago. She was wondering about the word apegapen. It's Dutch for being utterly exhausted.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Curious about words, right to the end.

segments.title: Border checks end, wider spot checks begin

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Now to the borders, and a change if you drive to Belgium or Germany.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The temporary border checks are over. They ended yesterday. They were run by the Koninklijke Marechaussee.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That's the Royal Military Police. It guards the borders, airports like Schiphol, and the royal family.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The checks were brought in in December 2024 by Marjolein Faber, asylum minister for Geert Wilders' far-right PVV in the previous cabinet. They were meant to last six months.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And they kept getting extended, which is unusual inside Schengen, the passport-free zone covering most of Europe.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Did they work?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Between December 2024 and March this year, about six hundred people were refused entry, mostly for lacking valid travel documents. Two hundred seventy were arrested, for things like document fraud and people smuggling. But the national audit office found the checks didn't reduce migration.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Asylum minister Bart van den Brink announced the end in May. The cabinet still wants to fight illegal migration and smuggling, but border towns, businesses and residents had complained about traffic disruption.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So what replaces them?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: From today, spot checks anywhere within twenty kilometres of the border, at changing times and places. Officers can stay on the same road for longer, and there's no more six-hour daily limit. On a selected train, they can check every passenger.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And the Marechaussee likes it. They say smugglers can no longer count on a checkpoint packing up after six hours.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: One practical note: Germany is keeping its own border checks until at least March next year.

segments.title: MPs balk at taxing small savers

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: To The Hague now, and the fight over taxing your savings.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Earlier this week we told you the cabinet wants to cut the tax-free return in box three, the savings and investment tax, to a thousand euros, pulling about eight hundred fifty thousand more people in.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Well, on the first day of the annual budget debate, MPs basically said: not like this.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The coalition of D66, VVD and CDA has no majority, and JA21, ChristenUnie, the SGP and Pro all oppose this. The SGP's Flach called it 'a fine on thrift'.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Now the coalition says it'll look at alternatives. But D66 insists any alternative raises the same money, four hundred seventy-three million euros, from taxing wealth. Pro suggests going after bigger fortunes.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Income tax is the other sore point. Both bands go up next year, and the Council of State, the government's top legal adviser, says nearly all the extra tax lands on workers. JA21 and Pro want that scaled back.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Finance Minister Heinen responds today. Separately, the cabinet also wants to nearly halve the current tax-free allowance next year, to about thirty-one thousand euros per person. That still needs both houses of parliament before the end of the year.

segments.title: Mortgage rates hit a high; estate agents face a register

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Staying with your wallet, mortgage rates have hit their highest level this year.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The average ten-year fixed rate with NHG, that's the government-backed mortgage guarantee, is now four and a half percent. Just a few weeks ago it was a little over four.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Is that the European Central Bank?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: No, the ECB's held steady. It's rates on the capital markets, where banks raise money, pushed up by worries about inflation, energy and geopolitics. And Dutch lending rules tie how much you can borrow to that rate. A couple earning ninety thousand can now borrow about three hundred ninety-five thousand euros. At three and a half percent, it was about four hundred thirteen.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So do prices come down?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Not for now. Demand still far outstrips supply. But Amsterdam is cooling. Prices there rose less than one percent in a year, against more than four nationally, and ABN Amro expects that cooling to spread.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Meanwhile, estate agents, the makelaars. Right now there's no government licence to be one. Housing Minister Boekholt-O'Sullivan of D66 wants every agent on a government register, with a disputes committee that can strike agents off in serious cases.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And buyers get to see the bidding log, the record of every bid. Big deal here, where you bid blind and often way over asking.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Almost a third of people surveyed had a bad experience with an agent. Only two percent ever complained. Concrete plans are due early next year.

segments.title: Tougher line on attacks against public workers

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Now, violence against police, paramedics and others who serve the public, and a much tougher line from prosecutors starting today.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: What's changing?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The Openbaar Ministerie, the national prosecution service, says every attack on someone in a public role now goes to court. That covers police, emergency workers, train staff, teachers, referees, journalists and more. No settling it with a fine or community service. Prosecutors must ask for double the usual sentence, with prison as the starting point.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Justice Minister David van Weel gave an example. A first offender tries to seriously assault an emergency worker, no weapon, no injury. That would in principle mean a three-month prison demand, instead of eighty hours of community service if the victim were anyone else.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Judges still decide, and prosecutors can adjust for circumstances. MPs pushed for this after New Year's Eve, when police and firefighters were attacked, sometimes lured into ambushes.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And on the same day, rail staff sounded the alarm.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The rail workers' union VVMC sent an urgent letter. NS, the national railway, has logged more than five thousand reports of aggression against staff so far this year. In all of 2023 it was under three thousand. Conductors have been knocked unconscious at Rotterdam Blaak and in Den Dolder.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The union wants more security on trains, and it wants back the enforcement powers senior conductors lost in 2022, when NS cut costs. NS says it's giving every conductor a body camera, testing batons for security staff, and hiring more.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: If you commute by train, that's a sobering set of numbers.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: In Amsterdam, a closely watched trial to treat crack addiction has suddenly been stopped.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: This was the one using an ADHD drug, right?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Dexamphetamine, yes. A bit like methadone for heroin users: a controlled stimulant to curb the cravings. A long-acting version was developed over twelve years by a project called REDUCE, whose partners include the city health service, the GGD.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So who pulled the plug?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The IGJ, the national health inspectorate. It stopped production of the medicine at a hospital it won't name. It says it's concerned about the medicine's quality, but it hasn't said what the problem is.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And people were already taking it?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The first participants were, and their treatment's been interrupted. Alexander Scholtes, the city's wethouder, or alderman, for health, says he can't say how many people are affected.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The city called the halt unexpected, and said the reasons are unclear. Scholtes says 'the only promising method' for heavily addicted people is now off the table. The GGD estimates there are three to nine thousand crack users in the city, many of them homeless or with mental health problems.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Scholtes and Mayor Femke Halsema wrote to Health Minister Sophie Hermans, asking her to review the decision and bring everyone together before the first of November.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: She's replied, but didn't commit to the meeting. She says the inspectorate is independent, and she has confidence in its judgment. The research team has until the end of the year to decide whether the study can go on.

segments.title: The Netherlands threatens to withhold money from Italy

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Back to Bart van den Brink, the asylum minister, who's now threatening to withhold money from Italy.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Withhold money for what?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Under EU rules, the country where an asylum seeker first enters the EU is usually responsible for them. Other countries can send people back there.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And a lot of people arrive in Italy across the Mediterranean. Italy has for years mostly refused to take them back.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: In June, Van den Brink went to Rome and signed a declaration with Italy's interior minister. Italy would again accept asylum seekers who travelled through Italy and applied here from the twelfth of June onwards.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That's when the new EU Migration Pact took effect. Under it, countries like the Netherlands help Mediterranean states, either by taking in asylum seekers or by paying. The Netherlands chose to pay. Its share of the EU's solidarity pot is about eleven million euros this year.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And in practice?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Very little. A European Commission report found that in the pact's first three weeks, Italy carried out none of the twelve transfer requests it got from EU countries. And Dutch courts keep blocking transfers. On the twenty-second of September, judges said the minister hadn't shown Italy had reception places ready.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So on Wednesday he told parliament, quote, 'If something doesn't work, we won't pay.' He plans to raise it with other EU ministers and the European Commission.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Money as leverage, then. Whether that moves Rome is another question.

segments.title: A Van Gogh heads for a record

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Sam, how's your art budget looking? Because a Van Gogh is coming up for sale.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Let me check. No.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Sotheby's expects 'Chestnut Trees in Blossom' to fetch about a hundred eighty million dollars in New York on the eighteenth of November. Maybe two hundred million or more.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The current Van Gogh auction record is a hundred seventeen million. So this would smash it.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: He painted it in May 1890, days after arriving in Auvers-sur-Oise, outside Paris. He died there two months later.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And hardly anyone's seen it in decades. An Argentine couple, Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier and sugar magnate Carlos Pedro Blaquier, bought it in 1975. It was last shown in public at the Guggenheim in 1964. Now their children are selling.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Sixty years out of sight. That's quite the comeback.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Meanwhile, here in Amsterdam, the Van Gogh Museum lets you stare at his work for the price of a ticket. Which, by my maths, is a slight saving.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Slight.

segments.title: Fabel Friet's queues and neighbours' house prices

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Speaking of what things are worth, back to the Nine Streets and a very famous chip shop.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Quick recap: residents took the city to court over Fabel Friet on Runstraat, and its daily TikTok queues, litter and crowds.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Now there's a study. Rosa van der Drift, a PhD candidate at TU Delft, looked at more than six thousand Amsterdam home sales. Homes within five hundred metres of the shop sold for almost five percent less than similar homes further away. That's about forty-one thousand euros.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And right up close?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Within seventy metres, more than eleven percent less.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Ouch. Though the study doesn't pin down why. And it covers 2015 to 2023, while the TikTok queues only started in 2022.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Fair point. A judge rules on the residents' case in a few weeks. Meanwhile an opinion piece in Het Parool told the complainers they're 'warmly welcome in Purmerend', a commuter town north of the city.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Brutal. Well, if queuing for fried food is your thing, there's a free option this weekend.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Saturday, four till nine, IJver on the old NDSM shipyard in Amsterdam-Noord is throwing an anniversary party. A thousand free oysters, a thousand free bitterballen, the deep-fried Dutch snack, and draught beer or spritz for two fifty.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Free entry, no sign-up. But the free food only lasts while supplies last, so don't dawdle.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Noted. Something more highbrow?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Chez Matisse opens Saturday at the H'ART Museum in the Plantage. More than eighty works by Henri Matisse, including La Blouse roumaine. Open ten to five, and it runs until mid-February, so no rush.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Then, Friday to Sunday at the Ziggo Dome in Zuidoost, Joe Hisaishi conducts the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra and plays piano. His Studio Ghibli scores, Spirited Away, Ponyo, Howl's Moving Castle, with film clips on a big screen.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It's the orchestra's first time at the Ziggo Dome. Practical tip: the run also has a Beethoven's Ninth night, so check you're booking the Ghibli one.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Unless you want Beethoven. No judgment. And tonight, Afrovibes kicks off its twenty-third edition at De Brakke Grond, the Flemish cultural centre in the city centre. Dance, theatre, music and spoken word from African and diaspora artists, on land, ancestry and belonging.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Tonight from seven fifteen, then Friday and Saturday from seven thirty. Over the weekend it also moves to the Bijlmer Parktheater and Framer Framed, though those Bijlmer dates may still change.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And Sunday, a slow one: the Sunday Market at Westergas in Westerpark. Street food, local makers, art, and a walk in the park after.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That's Dutch Daily Briefing for Thursday. Our thoughts are with Paulien Cornelisse's family.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Have a good day, wherever you're cycling. See you tomorrow.
